The <ACTOR> loader implements itself with the name Security Support Provider, a legitimate Windows function. Various <ACTOR> .exe files mimic legitimate file names used by Microsoft, Symantec, Kaspersky, Hewlett-Packard, and VMWare. <ACTOR> also disguised malicious modules using similar filenames as custom network encryption software on victims.
The <ACTOR> main executable has disguised itself as Microsoft’s Narrator.
The PowerShell script with the <ACTOR> payload was obfuscated using the COMPRESS technique in `Invoke-Obfuscation`.
To move laterally on a victim network, <ACTOR> has used credentials stolen from various systems on which it gathered usernames and password hashes.

Using AppleScript, <ACTOR> adds it's executable to the user's `~/.zshrc_aliases` file (`"echo " & payload & " > ~/zshrc_aliases"`), it then adds a line to the .zshrc file to source the `.zshrc_aliases` file (`[ -f $HOME/.zshrc_aliases ] && . $HOME/.zshrc_aliases`). Each time the user starts a new `zsh` terminal session, the `.zshrc` file executes the `.zshrc_aliases` file.
Using the machine's local time, <ACTOR> waits 43200 seconds (12 hours) from the initial creation timestamp of a specific file, .report. After the elapsed time, <ACTOR> executes additional modules.
